title: Runbook Automation Tools: 6 Compared (2026 Guide)
summary: Runbook automation tools vary by execution method: on-premise, cloud, or hybrid. Compare seven options to decide which one fits your infrastructure needs.
body_markdown:
## Activepieces


Activepieces fits the runbooks that incident.io and a server tool leave over. These are the ones whose steps are app actions, like posting a notification, opening a ticket, updating a record, or calling an API. It doesn't run commands on hosts.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run it in production.


### Where it fits


For this kind of runbook, the cost math is simple. A step that sends a message or updates a ticket is cheap to run, and the expense comes from how many of those steps you chain and how often they fire.


That shape is what Activepieces is built for: a no-code builder where each step is a connector or an HTTP request, and a trigger starts the flow.


The connector list is a directory you can count:` packages/pieces/community` in the open-source monorepo holds 750 integrations, roughly 60% of them community-contributed, so a ticketing or chat tool your runbook needs is likely already there.


If it isn't, AI can generate the missing connector, and you can keep it as a private piece on your own instance rather than waiting on a vendor release.


Its self-hosted core is MIT-licensed, so if you run it on your own infrastructure the per-run charge falls away and you pay for the machine and whoever patches it.


Confirm the current tiers on its pricing page before you budget. Hosted plans are listed there, but I didn't re-check them for this integration.


Anything that hides the number behind a sales call isn't worth modeling, and that's a fair test to apply to every tool here.


### A cleanup example


Take cleanup after an incident. In the workflow shown below, an "Instance Stopped" trigger flows into a "Revoke Token" step, an HTTP request that POSTs to Square's OAuth revoke endpoint with an Authorization header and a body.


Look at the run details: both steps show green checkmarks and a "Run succeeded" message.


That tells you two things: the flow executed end to end, and the input and output of each step are inspectable, so someone who didn't build it can see what was sent and what came back.


### What it lacks


Don't expect native server orchestration. Its 750 integrations are connectors to apps and APIs, so Activepieces won't run a script on a fleet of hosts, manage inventory, or handle privilege and rollback the way a server-side tool does.


It also lacks on-call features: no schedules, escalation policies, or paging logic of the kind incident tooling provides.


So it ranks behind the dedicated tools for both jobs. Use it as glue beside them, where an incident or a server event needs to reach a ticket, a chat channel, or a business system without anyone writing a custom integration.
